paragraphs: Bharata was a mighty emperor; India is called Bharata Varsha after him. Following the old Hindu ideal that in later life one should hand over worldly duties and retire to meditate on the Self, he gave his throne to his son. The man who had ruled millions and lived in marble palaces built himself a reed-and-grass hut by a Himalayan river, lived on roots and herbs he gathered himself, and meditated on the Lord within.

Years passed. One day a pregnant deer came to drink near where he sat. Suddenly a lion roared nearby. Terrified, she leapt across the river, gave birth to a fawn mid-flight and died. The newborn fell into the rushing water. Bharata jumped up, pulled it out, carried it home and warmed it back to life by his fire.

He raised the fawn on soft grass and fruit, and it grew into a beautiful deer. But the man who had walked away from an empire and family now became attached to this deer. The fonder he grew, the less he could focus on God. If it came home late from grazing, he worried it had met a tiger. When death came, his last thoughts were on the deer's sad eyes, not on the Self. So he was reborn as a deer, though one that remembered its past life and always grazed near hermitages where the Upanishads were chanted.

Next he was born as the youngest son of a rich Brahmin. Remembering everything, he resolved never to get entangled again. He grew up strong but never spoke, living as if dull and simple. When their father died, his brothers took his share, gave him just enough food, and their wives worked him hard and treated him harshly. He never complained; when it got too much, he sat under a tree until things calmed down.

One day the king of the land came by in a palanquin, short one bearer. The servants grabbed the sturdy young man and put the pole on his shoulder. Trying not to step on tiny creatures on the road, Bharata walked unevenly, and the king leaned out and called him a fool, telling him to rest if his shoulders hurt. Then Bharata set down the pole and spoke for the first time. Whom was the king calling a fool, or tired? The body is matter like the king's own; the mind is universal; and the true Self never tires, never weakens, and never carried any pole. He spoke beautifully about the soul and the highest knowledge.

The king, proud of his own learning, stepped down and fell at Bharata's feet, begging forgiveness. Bharata blessed him and went back to his quiet life. When he left his body, he was free forever from the cycle of birth.
learn: Attachment can sneak in through something small and sweet, even after we have given up big things. Watch where your mind keeps drifting. And never judge someone's depth by their silence or their job.
